extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimentalists, gunners, instrument-makers, and Royal Society readers (17th-century scientists and engineers)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical and practical rules for solving projectile-motion problems and for conducting/ reporting gunnery experiments (including geometric constructions, velocity/force at points of the trajectory, and when to account for air resistance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest altitude of perpendicular projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest altitude of the perpendicular projection is a 4th of the parameter, or half the greatest horizontal range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct geometric/analytic relation (versed sine of 180° being = 2r) used in computations of projectile maxima.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of flight proportional to sine of elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The lines GF, or times of the flight of a project cast with the same degree of velocity at different elevations, are as the sines of the elevations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the projected line lengths are proportional to sines of elevation and times are proportional to those lines, thus times vary as sines — use this when comparing flight times at different elevations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to find parameter and velocity from distance/height/angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the distance and altitude or descent of an object through which the projectile passes, together with the angle of elevation of the line of direction, find the parameter and velocity by proportional relations involving secants and tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct GL and LM from given data (GM = distance, MX = height/descent); LX (fall) relates via the parabola so GL:parameter::LX:GL etc. Find time in seconds for a free fall through LX and divide GL by that time to obtain the velocity (space per second). The velocity obtained is a mean proportional between the parameter and 16 feet (1 inch reference in the original units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule to compute elevations to hit a given object (two possible elevations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Having the parameter, the horizontal distance, and height or descent of an object, the required elevation(s) (angles) are roots of a quadratic relating tangent t, horizontal distance b, altitude/descent h, and parameter p; the equation yields two answers (upper and lower elevations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic rule: divide half the parameter by the horizontal distance (reserve quotient); form the sum/difference of that quotient with the square-root expression derived from (half_parameter)^2 ± ph and bb terms — these give the tangents of the required elevations. Practical notes: if tangent exceed quotient in descents the lower direction is below the horizon; if discriminant = 0 there is one elevation; if discriminant < 0 the object is out of reach. From 4bb + 4ph = pp one determines the utmost limits of reach. Also gives method to find least parameter/velocity needed to reach object (using semiparameter and dividing by b). Useful specifically for bombadiers and gunners to avoid excess powder and increase certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical construction for finding elevations
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric construction equivalent to the analytic solution: make right angle and lengths DA, DF = p (parameter), DG = b (horizontal distance), DB/DC = h (perpendicular height); draw GB, make DE equal to GB; with radius AC and centre E sweep arc to intersect AD in H; laying off DH both ways from F gives K and L; lines GL and GK give the elevations LGD and KGD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction notes: when the object is below the horizon lay its descent from A so AC = AD + DC; if in descents K may fall below D indicating depression. This construction follows naturally from the analytic equation and is offered for practical/graphical use by gunners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity/force at every point of the trajectory (tangent rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocity of a projectile at any point of its parabola is compounded of the impressed constant horizontal velocity and the acquired vertical (fall) velocity; velocities at points are proportional to lengths of tangents to the parabola intercepted between any two diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely: in a given time the descent gives a velocity equal to twice the descent (equable-motion equivalence); drawing GZ (as per figure), the velocity at X is to the impressed velocity at G as GZ is to GL. Thus comparative force at two points can be discovered geometrically or arithmetically. Corollaries: force is least at the vertex V; equal at equal distances from vertex; ratio of least force at V to that at G or B equals radius to secant of elevation angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to neglect air resistance and when not to
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytic rules for projectile motion would be rigidly true were it not for resistance of the medium (air); however, for large heavy shot resistance is scarcely discernible, while for small/light shot resistance must be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical guidance: weight of air relative to water ~1:800, so resistance relative to shot weight can be estimated; resistance likely scales reciprocally with shot specific gravity and diameter (for same velocity and size different matter) and may scale with diameter reciprocally for same material; whether resistance varies as velocity or its square is uncertain. Practical experiments showed large solid brass shots (~14 lb, 44-inch—OCR likely odd) had upper and lower ranges nearly equal; smaller shot showed under (lower) ranges exceed upper, implying air resistance effects more for light/small projectiles. Account for experimental errors from powder variability, shot fit, and carriage looseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method and reporting for gunnery trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform controlled trials (e.g., mortarpiece fixed to earth) and repeat experiments with variations (barrel length, shot size) and report observed differences and likely causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report comparative results (e.g., ranges above/below 45°), note if differences are less than ordinary practice errors; when differences are small state they may be due to experimental inadequacy. Repeat and vary parameters to assess influence (e.g., barrel length was found to have little advantage in Papin's rarefaction trials). Present experiments to learned body (Royal Society) and record limitations candidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and operation of a rarefaction-based shooting apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: A pipe AA (uniform bore) with small side pipe BB connected to pneumatic engine; pipe closed by outward valves; lead piece D fitted to bore and driven by atmospheric pressure when valve suddenly opened after exhausting the pipe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction notes: support pipe (CC), fit lead to bore (D), shut pipe at both ends with outward valves to allow exhausting; when opening valve toward D suddenly, atmospheric pressure drives D rapidly. For large bores the aperture toward D may be much smaller than the pipe because high air velocity through a smaller aperture can press the lead nearly as effectively as if the whole bore were open. Empirical result: force comparable to compression wind-gun; increasing barrel length gave little additional effect in trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colour table to describe natural colours
rubrics_metrics.description: A table of simple and mixed colours is given so one can identify which simple ingredients compose a mixed colour: ingredient above for one component and ingredient at the side for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation: to describe a plant or natural object's colour, find the nearest simple or mixed colour in the table and use the word affixed to that colour. The table mixes each simple yellow/red with each simple blue to form most medium colours (greens, purples, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions and preparation notes for pigment materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Short descriptions/preparation methods for many pigments (cerusse, masticot, gutta gambae/gambogia, ochre, orpiment, umber, red-lead, burned ochre, cinnabar/vermillion, carmine, lake, sanguis draconis, lamp-black, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipes and provenance notes: e.g., cerusse (white lead) is produced by vaporous calcination and made in plumbers' shops by laying lead plates over strong vinegar; masticot is a calx of lead; cinnabar has native and factitious kinds (sublimation of mercury and sulfur). Use these preparation notes when identifying or preparing pigments and when describing their historical uses. Warnings: some pigments (orpiment) are poisonous/corrosive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for computing ephemerides and astronomical tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Ephemerides for the year were computed from astronomers' own tables whose numbers, by many years observation, are found to answer with great preciseness to celestial motions, except the moon whose motion has manifold inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: compute places from internally consistent tables validated by observation; reduce moon's place tymchonic to local meridian and compute true latitudes; continue series over years to increase value to astronomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting geographic/astronomical observations on journeys
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting on journeys (e.g., imperial progresses), include latitudes, magnetic declinations, instruments carried, and observations of meteors and physical features; measure heights and distances with mathematical instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical notes from the journey account: bring instruments and personnel to record pole elevation and magnetic declination at places visited; record latitudes, local declination values (e.g., 41°56' lat; needle declination 0° at Xin-Yam; 44°20' lat; needle declination south to west 1°40' at Ula), and describe roads/engineering observed (e.g., road width, levelling, bridges, ornamental mats).
